lesson.title: Slope: Measuring How Steeply a Line Climbs
lesson.summary: Slope is the constant rate of change of a line, calculated as the ratio of vertical change to horizontal change between any two points on that line.
lesson.body:
The linear function chapter showed that a defining feature of any linear relationship is a constant rate of change: the output climbs by the exact same amount for every unit increase in input. Slope is the formal name for that rate of change, and it is calculated using any two points on the line's graph, (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), with the formula slope = (y2 - y1) divided by (x2 - x1). The numerator measures vertical change, and the denominator measures horizontal change, so slope compares how much a line rises against how much it runs, packaging both directions into a single number. A large positive slope describes a line that climbs steeply from left to right, a small positive slope describes a gentle uphill climb, a negative slope describes a line that falls from left to right, and a slope of exactly zero describes a perfectly flat, horizontal line.

Slope can be calculated using any two distinct points on a line, and the result will always be the same number, because the rate of change is constant along the entire line by definition. This is a powerful check: if two different pairs of points on the same line produce two different slope values, something was calculated incorrectly, since a straight line cannot have a changing steepness partway through, only a curve could do that. It also does not matter which of the two points gets labeled (x1, y1) and which gets labeled (x2, y2), as long as the same order is used consistently in both the numerator and the denominator, since reversing both signs together leaves the final ratio unchanged.

Here is a worked example using the familiar line y = 3x - 2, which already has several known points from earlier chapters: (0, -2), (1, 1), and (2, 4). Using the first and third points, (0, -2) and (2, 4), the slope is (4 - (-2)) divided by (2 - 0), which equals 6 divided by 2, or 3. Now check this using a different pair of points, (1, 1) and (2, 4): the slope is (4 - 1) divided by (2 - 1), which equals 3 divided by 1, or 3. Both calculations agree on a slope of 3, confirming the line has a constant rate of change of 3, which also matches the coefficient of x in the original equation y = 3x - 2, exactly as it should.

That match is not a coincidence. In slope-intercept form, y = mx + b, the letter m always represents the slope directly, the same way b always represents the y-intercept. Recognizing an equation in this form lets you read off the slope immediately, without picking any points or doing any subtraction at all, which is one reason slope-intercept form is used so often for quick graphing and comparison of lines.

The vertical change in the numerator of the slope formula has its own name, rise, and the horizontal change in the denominator has its own name, run. Splitting slope into these two separately named pieces, covered in the next two chapters, makes it easier to talk about vertical and horizontal movement individually before combining them back into the single ratio that describes a line's steepness.
